This is where a genuine gap first becomes visible and where a small number of well-targeted sessions does the most work per dirham, because misconceptions are still single and identifiable.
programmes.countryNote: The most common Dubai referral at this stage is a child who was fine in Year 2 and stalled in Year 3, which is almost always the transition from counting strategies to recall and place-value reasoning. Four to six sessions on one strand typically settles it.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme, upper primary
programmes.description: Fractions, decimals and percentages as one connected idea, proportional reasoning, area and volume, data handling and early probability. Costs rise here because the content genuinely needs a teacher, and because a gap left from Year 3 now shows up in four different topics at once.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families often start spending in Year 6, driven by the move to the Middle Years Programme or to a British Year 7. That is late but not too late; six to ten sessions on fractions and proportional reasoning is the highest-value block available at primary age.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Criterion-referenced marking out of eight, a split into standard and extended routes around Year 10, and a jump in the amount of reasoning students must write down. Primary gaps that were invisible become expensive here, which is the honest financial case for spending something in Year 5 or 6.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the Year 7 intake at continuum schools mixes children from several primary systems, and teachers spend the first term finding gaps. A child who arrives fluent in number facts and comfortable with fractions is rarely the one who needs paid support in Year 8.

dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.subjectsIntro: Primary maths is not one subject, and the cost of fixing a problem depends entirely on which part of it is broken. These are the areas we work on, with how quickly each one responds and therefore what it costs.

subjects.name: Number sense and place value
subjects.description: Understanding what the digits mean, not just reading them. A child who cannot say what happens to 304 when you take ten away has a place-value gap, and it will surface again in subtraction, decimals and rounding. Responds fast: three or four sessions plus short daily practice.

subjects.name: Addition and subtraction strategies
subjects.description: Bridging ten, compensation, partitioning, and subtracting across a zero. Most Dubai referrals at this age are here. The cheapest fix is usually a method made explicit once and then practised at home for ten minutes a day, which is tutoring at its most cost-effective.

subjects.name: Multiplication, division and number facts
subjects.description: Recall and the reasoning behind it. Fluency is a practice problem rather than a teaching problem, so paying an adult AED 200 an hour to drill tables is poor value. A tutor is worth it for the structure, division with remainders, and the link to fractions.

subjects.name: Fractions, decimals and percentages
subjects.description: The single highest-value strand to buy help with at primary age, because the three are one idea and most children are taught them as three. A gap here is the most reliable predictor of struggle in the first year of the Middle Years Programme. Expect six to ten sessions.

subjects.name: Pattern and function
subjects.description: Early algebra: sequences, rules, relationships, the unknown as a quantity rather than a missing box. Slowest strand to move and the one most dependent on a teacher spotting the misconception, which makes it the strand where a cheap tutor is a false economy.

subjects.name: Measurement
subjects.description: Standard units, conversion, perimeter, area, volume, time. Conversion errors in Dubai classrooms often come from mixed exposure to metric and imperial at home. Usually quick to fix and a good first strand for a family testing whether tutoring helps at all.

subjects.name: Shape and space
subjects.description: Properties, angles, symmetry, position and transformation. Visual and often a strength for children who struggle elsewhere, which makes it useful early in a block for rebuilding a child's belief that they can do mathematics.

subjects.name: Data handling and probability
subjects.description: Reading and making graphs, averages, early chance. Cheap to fix and frequently the strand where a child loses marks in an entrance assessment despite understanding the maths, because the question is about reading the axis rather than calculating.

subjects.name: Mathematical language and word problems
subjects.description: Turning sentences into operations. For Dubai's large population of children learning in English as an additional language, this is frequently the real problem being misread as a maths problem, and it needs a tutor who can tell the difference.

subjects.name: Mental calculation fluency
subjects.description: Speed and confidence with facts held in memory. The clearest case in all of primary maths for an app or a parent with flashcards rather than a paid hour. We will say so in the first lesson if that is what the diagnosis shows.

dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.regionsTitle: Dubai communities, the four o'clock problem and what it costs
dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.regionsIntro: For a primary-age child the binding constraint is not money, it is the half-hour window between getting home and losing the ability to concentrate. These notes cover when that window falls in different parts of Dubai, and what it means for what you pay.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Short school runs for families whose children attend nearby, so a 3.45pm session is realistic and a young child is still fresh. That matters financially: a 25-minute session that lands in the good window achieves more than a bought hour at 6pm, at roughly half the cost.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Al Barsha South
regions.note: Dense school provision and generally short journeys, but heavy after-school club participation. Families here often find Thursday the only clear day, and a single longer weekly session on one strand is the sensible purchase rather than two scattered slots.

regions.name: Jumeirah Golf Estates and Dubai Sports City
regions.note: Training schedules dominate the late afternoon for many children. A morning weekend slot is usually better value than a weekday evening, because a tired seven-year-old at 6.30pm produces almost nothing a parent is paying for.

regions.name: Al Khawaneej and Mirdif
regions.note: Longer journeys from central Dubai schools, which pushes the window past 5pm and makes short sessions essential rather than optional. Online delivery removes the tutor's travel from the equation entirely, which is where the in-home premium mostly goes.

regions.name: Business Bay and Downtown Dubai
regions.note: Apartment living with working parents nearby, so a parent can often attend the first session without taking leave. Worth doing once for a primary child, because what you are really assessing is whether the tutor can hold a nine-year-old's attention.

regions.name: Mudon, Town Square and Dubailand
regions.note: Younger families with several children close in age, which makes the sibling-sharing question live. Our honest answer is in the table below: it halves the rate and halves the value, and two separate 25-minute slots usually cost the same as one shared hour.

regions.name: Dubai Creek Harbour and Al Jaddaf
regions.note: Newer communities with a high proportion of families recently arrived in the PYP. First-year parents here spend most on tutoring and need it least; a term of reading the school's own reporting usually answers the question for free.

regions.name: Dubai South and The Sustainable City
regions.note: Longer distances and limited local tutor supply, which is where an in-home arrangement becomes both expensive and unreliable. One-to-one live video costs the same here as in Jumeirah, which is the clearest practical case for the format.

schoolClusters.city: Central and western Dubai primary provision
schoolClusters.note: Students we support in these communities are usually at schools with established PYP maths practice and good intervention groups, which means the free option should be tried first. Where families still come to us it is most often for fractions in Years 5 and 6, or for a specific place-value gap identified by the class teacher.

schoolClusters.city: Eastern and southern Dubai primary provision
schoolClusters.note: A wider spread of curricula, and more children moving between systems mid-primary. Students we support from these areas more often need the mathematical language work rather than the mathematics, because a change of system changes the vocabulary of the questions before it changes the content.

sections.heading: What a Dubai maths hour buys at each published price point
paragraphs: The published rate ladder in this emirate is wide and badly explained, so here it is with what each rung actually delivers for a primary child. At the bottom, EdFlik advertises online tuition from AED 45 to AED 65 per hour and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to AED 52, generally using university students and recent graduates. In the middle, Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB tuition from AED 200. TutorChase lists AED 270 per hour for specialist support. Bestimate's Dubai rate survey reports in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 and specialist exam-year help at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with BartyED advertising AED 650 for premium named tutors. Those are other providers' published figures, read in October 2026, and none of them are IB Gram prices.

For a nine-year-old with a place-value gap, the difference between the rungs is diagnostic skill rather than subject knowledge. Everyone on that ladder can do primary arithmetic. Not everyone can watch a child subtract 304 minus 10, see that they are counting back rather than reasoning about the tens digit, and know which of four possible misconceptions is in play. That is a trained primary teacher's skill and it is the whole value proposition at the upper rates. A cheaper tutor will reteach the method the school already taught, which the child will follow in the session and fail at again on Tuesday.

The honest arithmetic follows from that. Six sessions at AED 200 that fix a misconception cost AED 1,200 and end. Twenty sessions at AED 50 that supervise homework cost AED 1,000 and do not end, because nothing was diagnosed. The cost per hour favours the second and the cost per fixed problem favours the first by a wide margin. The exception is genuine: if the problem is purely fluency, the cheap tutor and the expensive tutor are equally unnecessary and a free app with a parent checking it beats both.

sections.heading: Costing it by strand: the five parts of PYP maths do not cost the same
paragraphs: PYP mathematics is organised into five strands: number, pattern and function, measurement, shape and space, and data handling. Buying tutoring without knowing which strand is broken is how Dubai families end up twelve sessions in with a child who is still stuck, because the sessions have been covering the strand that was never the problem.

The strands respond at very different speeds and therefore cost very different amounts to fix. Measurement conversion errors and data-handling misreadings are usually two or three sessions. A place-value gap is three or four, plus daily practice. Fractions, decimals and percentages treated as one connected idea is six to ten, and it is the best money anyone spends at primary age because it is the strongest predictor of difficulty in the first Middle Years year. Pattern and function is the slowest and the most teacher-dependent, because the misconceptions are conceptual rather than procedural.

What this means practically is that you should buy one strand. Not a term of maths, not general support, one strand, with an agreed end point. Our session notes name the strand and the specific misconception being addressed, which is what lets a parent see that the money is going where they decided it should. A provider who cannot tell you which strand they are working on this week is selling hours rather than teaching. The table below applies the mid-market figure of AED 200 an hour, which is where Unitors' published IB rate starts, to each strand. Read it as arithmetic on somebody else's quoted rate rather than as our price list, and use it to sanity-check any quote you are given, including ours.

sections.heading: The cheaper options, costed honestly
paragraphs: A tutoring page that never recommends not buying tutoring is advertising. There are four cheaper options for a Dubai primary maths worry and at least two of them are better than a paid hour for the most common problems. They are listed below with real costs and real limits, and we will point a family at any of them in the free first lesson if the diagnosis says so.

The school's own intervention group is first for a reason. It costs nothing, it is run by someone who sees your child every day, and KHDA-inspected schools in Dubai generally have a functioning referral process. The thing to ask for is specific: not extra help, but which strand the school thinks is weak and what the intervention will target. A school that cannot answer that is a reason to look outside; a school that answers it well has just done your diagnosis for free.

Fluency apps are second, and genuinely effective for the single most common primary complaint. If the problem is that a child knows how to multiply but is slow and loses confidence, ten minutes a day on a structured practice app for a few dirhams a month will do more than an adult at AED 200 an hour. The honest limit is that an app cannot find a misconception; it will drill a wrong method as cheerfully as a right one. That is exactly where a single diagnostic session earns its keep and a block of twenty does not.

sections.heading: Where Dubai families actually waste money on primary maths
paragraphs: Four patterns account for most of the wasted spending we see, and none of them are about choosing a bad tutor. The first is buying a term. A term is a unit of school administration, not a unit of teaching, and a child with a measurement gap needs three sessions rather than twelve. Providers sell terms because terms are predictable revenue. Families buy them because the alternative requires a diagnosis nobody offered.

The second is paying an adult to drill. Number-fact fluency is a repetition problem and repetition is the cheapest commodity in education. Watching a tutor at AED 200 an hour run times tables with a nine-year-old is the clearest waste in this market, and it is extremely common because it looks like work and the child does get faster. They would have got faster for free.

The third is starting too early. A worried parent of a five-year-old is usually responding to a developmental range rather than a problem, and paid intervention at that age mostly buys the parent reassurance. The fourth is starting too late in a different sense: leaving a fractions gap from Year 5 until the second term of Year 7, by which point it is showing up across four topics and costs three times as much to close. Spending in Year 6 is the single best-timed primary purchase in Dubai, and spending in Year 1 is usually the worst. A fifth pattern deserves a mention because it is invisible to the family paying for it: booking the only slot left rather than the right one. A nine-year-old at 6.30pm after a long school run produces perhaps ten useful minutes, whatever the tutor charges for the hour.

sections.heading: Why the PYP report has no percentage, and how to read it for spending decisions
paragraphs: Dubai parents who grew up with marks out of a hundred find PYP reporting genuinely hard to act on. There are no examinations and no percentages. Reporting describes what a child can do against learning outcomes and conceptual understandings, often in sentences that sound uniformly positive. A report saying a child is developing an understanding of fractions could describe a child two months behind or a child comfortably on track, and the sentence is identical.

The way to extract a spending decision from it is to ask three specific questions at the next parent meeting, in writing if necessary. Which of the five strands is weakest for my child. What specifically does she do when she gets a question in that strand wrong. And what is the school already doing about it. A teacher who sees your child daily can answer all three in five minutes, and the answers are a better diagnosis than any paid assessment, because they are based on months of observation rather than one session.

Those answers also change what you should buy. If the teacher says the strand is number and the error is counting back rather than reasoning about place value, that is three or four sessions on one thing. If the teacher says the maths is fine but the child cannot get started on a word problem, the issue is mathematical language, which is a different tutor and often a different subject entirely. If the teacher cannot name a strand or an error, that is itself information, and a single diagnostic session is then worth more than a term of anything.

sections.heading: Transdisciplinary maths, and why the homework looks nothing like yours
paragraphs: In the PYP, a good deal of mathematics is taught inside units of inquiry rather than as a separate subject, with stand-alone teaching alongside it. So a Dubai parent may see their Year 4 child measuring shadows for a unit about light and conclude that no mathematics is being taught. Measurement, data handling and often shape and space are being taught, in a context the child will remember. What is harder to see from outside is whether the underlying number work is being practised to fluency.

That design has a practical consequence for tutoring. A tutor who ignores the school's units and runs a parallel curriculum confuses the child and wastes the connection the school has built. A tutor who works only inside the units never gets to the fluency practice that transdisciplinary teaching does not naturally provide. The useful arrangement is a tutor who asks what the current unit is, uses its context where it fits, and does the number work separately and explicitly.

It also affects how a parent reads progress. Mathematics that appears in a unit of inquiry is assessed in the context of that unit, so a child can look confident in the measuring task and still be shaky on conversion in isolation. Asking a child to do the same operation out of context is a cheap and reliable test that any parent can run, and it frequently explains a mismatch between a warm school report and a struggle with homework.

sections.heading: What the spend is actually buying later: Checkpoint, MYP and the Year 7 step
paragraphs: The financial case for primary maths spending is not about Year 4. It is about what a gap costs later, and the costs are very unevenly distributed across the strands. A measurement gap in Year 4 is a measurement gap in Year 7, closed in two sessions whenever anyone notices. A fractions gap in Year 5 becomes, by Year 8, a problem in ratio, algebra, probability and percentage change simultaneously, and closing it then takes three times as long because four topics have to be revisited.

Some Dubai schools also use Cambridge Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests, which Cambridge International runs in March, May and October. Where a school uses them, they are a useful external reading in a programme that otherwise provides none, and worth asking about rather than worrying about. They are diagnostic rather than high-stakes, and no tutoring is required to sit them.

The step into Middle Years mathematics is where primary spending either pays or does not. The programme marks against four criteria out of eight and asks students to write reasoning down, which primary rarely demands. A child who arrives fluent in number facts, comfortable converting between fractions, decimals and percentages, and used to showing a method will handle the transition. That is a short, specific list, and it is exactly what a well-targeted Year 6 block should be built around rather than general confidence. Families moving instead to a British Year 7 in Dubai face a similar but shorter list, since written method and fluency matter there too and the fractions work is identical. Either way, the target is three or four specific capabilities rather than a general sense that the child is ready.

sections.heading: Home tutoring for a primary child in Dubai, and the honest trade
paragraphs: The case for a visiting tutor is strongest at primary age and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. A six-year-old works better with an adult physically beside them, concrete materials on the table, and no screen to look away from. The Dubai market serves this: Bestimate's survey reports in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 per hour, with monthly in-home packages of AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions in circulation. Those are other providers' published figures with their reading date.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE. Visiting tutors are a service we operate only in India, and we would rather say that plainly than take a booking and explain later. For every UAE family lessons are one-to-one on live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. Two honest points in favour: the travel premium disappears from the hour, and a 25-minute session becomes practical, which for a seven-year-old is the right length and is not economic for a tutor who has driven across Dubai to deliver it.

The genuine limits are worth stating. A child under about six is a poor fit for video, and we will say so rather than take the booking. A child who needs physical manipulatives can use household objects with a parent nearby for the first few sessions, which works but asks something of the parent. And a child who will not engage with a screen without an adult present is a real case for in-home, which we do not provide in this market. The table sets the trade out without pretending the choice is obvious.

sections.heading: Permits, the regulator and the things we will not claim
paragraphs: Three facts belong on any Dubai tutoring page and are missing from most of them. Private tutoring in the UAE is permit-regulated: the private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount appears here, and the official route is the service page titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing on mohre.gov.ae.

Second, the regulator. KHDA is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai, per the UAE government's own information service. Abu Dhabi has ADEK, Sharjah the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah its Department of Knowledge, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. IB Gram holds no permit, accreditation, licence or partnership from any of them, or from the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and claims none. A phrase implying regulator approval is the most common misrepresentation in this market.

Third, Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, per KHDA's mandatory-subjects guidelines, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes strictly prohibited. Those subjects take timetable hours in the same primary week as mathematics, which is a scheduling fact families should count when planning a session, and a reason the four o'clock window is as tight as it is.

process.title: Ask the class teacher three questions first
process.description: Which strand is weakest, what specifically does my child do when a question in it goes wrong, and what is the school already doing. Those three answers are free, based on months of observation, and better than any paid assessment. Bring them to us and the first session starts from a diagnosis rather than a guess.

process.title: Free 25-minute first lesson
process.description: Short, because that is the right length for a primary child, and free with no card details taken. The tutor works with your child on the suspected strand and tells you what they saw. If the answer is ten minutes of daily practice and no tutor, we will say that.

process.title: Buy one strand with an end point
process.description: Not a term. One strand, an agreed number of sessions, and a stated signal that means it is finished. For measurement that might be three sessions; for fractions it might be eight. You get the number, the strand and the end condition in writing before anything is paid.

process.title: Match on primary experience
process.description: Teaching mathematics to a nine-year-old is a different craft from teaching Diploma mathematics, and a strong Diploma tutor is often a poor primary one. Because delivery is online across the UAE we match on primary training rather than on who lives near your community.

process.title: Ten minutes a day between sessions
process.description: Every session sets a short home practice task, because fluency is built by repetition and repetition is free. The session note names the task and the strand. Families who do the ten minutes need fewer paid sessions, which is the opposite of how packages are usually designed.

process.title: Stop at the end condition
process.description: When the agreed signal appears, the block ends and we say so. If a new strand surfaces later, start another short block then. There is no rolling commitment, no minimum term and no automatic renewal, and we would rather you came back in Year 6 than paid continuously through Year 3.

whyPoints.title: Priced by strand, not by term
whyPoints.description: You buy one part of mathematics with an agreed end point, because a measurement gap is three sessions and a fractions gap is eight. A term is a unit of school administration, not a unit of teaching, and selling terms is how families end up twelve sessions into the wrong strand.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you not to buy
whyPoints.description: If the diagnosis is number-fact fluency, the honest answer is ten minutes of daily practice and no paid adult, and the free first lesson will say so. A meaningful share of Dubai families leave with a practice routine and no booking, which costs us an invoice and is still the right advice.

whyPoints.title: Short sessions, priced as short sessions
whyPoints.description: Twenty-five minutes twice a week beats one hour for a seven-year-old, and online delivery makes it economic because nobody has driven across Dubai to deliver it. Most providers resist this format because it is administratively inconvenient, not because it works less well.

whyPoints.title: Primary training, matched from the whole pool
whyPoints.description: Teaching mathematics to a nine-year-old is its own skill, and the scarce thing is not subject knowledge but the ability to see which of four misconceptions produced a wrong answer. Online delivery means we match on that rather than on driving distance.

whyPoints.title: No claims we cannot support
whyPoints.description: No regulator endorses IB Gram and we claim none. No grade promises, no success rates, no statistics without a source. Where this page states a regulatory fact it names the authority and the document, and where it states a rate it names the provider who published it.

faqs.question: What should one hour of PYP maths tutoring cost in Dubai, and what should be inside it?
faqs.answer: Published rates in this market run from AED 33 to AED 65 at the budget end, AED 150 to AED 270 for qualified and specialist tutors, and AED 650 for premium named tutors, all read in October 2026 from those providers' own pages. For a primary child the hour should contain a named strand, a diagnosis of the specific error your child makes in it, an explicit method, and a short home practice task. If the hour is homework supervision, you are paying a diagnostic rate for a babysitting service.

faqs.question: Why would I pay AED 200 for a seven-year-old's maths when tutors advertise at AED 45?
faqs.answer: Only for diagnosis. Everyone on the published rate ladder can do primary arithmetic; not everyone can watch a child subtract 304 minus 10 and see that they are counting back rather than reasoning about the tens digit. Six sessions at AED 200 that fix a misconception cost AED 1,200 and end. Twenty sessions at AED 45 that reteach the school's method cost AED 900 and do not end. If the problem is purely fluency, neither is the right purchase and daily practice is.

faqs.question: Is a 25-minute session better value than an hour for a child in Year 2?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and twice a week better still. A six or seven-year-old's useful concentration on mathematics runs out well before sixty minutes, so a bought hour frequently contains twenty-five minutes of teaching and thirty-five minutes of management. Two short sessions also shorten the gap between teaching and practice, which is where young children forget. The format only works economically online, because no tutor can justify crossing Dubai for twenty-five minutes, which is part of why in-home providers sell hours.

faqs.question: Our report says my daughter is a confident mathematician - why is she slow at mental arithmetic?
faqs.answer: Because PYP reporting describes conceptual understanding and does not measure recall speed, and the two are genuinely separate. A child can reason well about why multiplication works and still be slow at retrieving six times seven. That is a practice problem, it is the most common primary complaint in Dubai, and it is the one thing a paid tutor is least needed for. Ten minutes a day on structured practice for six weeks closes it, and a diagnostic session is only worth buying if you are unsure that is the real issue.

faqs.question: Which maths strand gives the best return on tutoring spend at primary age?
faqs.answer: Fractions, decimals and percentages, taught as one connected idea, in Years 5 and 6. It costs six to ten sessions and it is the strongest predictor of difficulty in the first year of the Middle Years Programme, where the same gap resurfaces simultaneously in ratio, algebra, probability and percentage change and takes three times as long to close. Measurement and data handling are cheap to fix at any age. Number-fact fluency should not be bought at all.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take my Year 3 and Year 6 children in the same booking to save money?
faqs.answer: The same tutor, yes, and some families prefer the continuity. The same session, no. A shared hour between children three years apart gives each of them half a session at a strand the other does not need, which halves the rate and more than halves the value. Two separate 25 or 30-minute slots typically cost about the same as one shared hour and produce two real diagnoses. For households in areas like Mudon and Town Square, where this comes up constantly, that is the honest arithmetic.

faqs.question: Is a maths app a cheaper substitute for a primary tutor in Dubai?
faqs.answer: For fluency, yes, and it is better as well as cheaper: a few dirhams a month and ten minutes a day beats a paid adult running times tables. For a misconception, no, because an app will drill a wrong method as cheerfully as a right one and will never notice. That is the whole case for a single diagnostic session: find out which problem you have, then use the cheapest tool that addresses it. A great many Dubai families need the app and not the block.

faqs.question: Does the school's own maths intervention group cost anything, and is it enough?
faqs.answer: It costs nothing and it is frequently enough, which is why we recommend trying it before buying anything. The thing to ask for is specific rather than general: which of the five strands the school thinks is weak, and what the intervention will target. A school that answers clearly has done your diagnosis for free. A school that cannot name a strand or an error has given you a different kind of information, and a single diagnostic session is then worth more than a term of anything.

faqs.question: How many weeks before I should expect to see something for the money?
faqs.answer: It depends on the strand, which is why we agree an end condition before starting. Measurement conversion or graph reading should look different within two or three sessions. A place-value method should hold on an unfamiliar question by session four, with daily practice in between. Fractions taught as one connected idea takes six to ten sessions and the change is gradual. If nothing has moved in four sessions on a strand that should respond quickly, that is a signal to change something rather than to buy more.

faqs.question: Do Dubai tutors charge more in the term before a school entrance assessment?
faqs.answer: Rates in this market are published annually rather than seasonally, so the quoted figures do not move. What moves is availability, and that has a cost of its own: the slots left in the weeks before a popular assessment window are the inconvenient ones, and families end up accepting a 6.30pm session for a nine-year-old, which is poor value at any rate. Booking a short block in a quiet month is cheaper in practice than booking the same block in a busy one.

faqs.question: Why does primary maths tutoring cost less than Diploma maths tutoring if teaching young children is harder?
faqs.answer: Because the market prices scarcity rather than difficulty. Published figures put IB support from AED 200 and specialist exam-year help at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, largely because the pool of adults who can teach Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is small and the perceived stakes are high. The pool who can teach primary number is far larger, even though the pool who can do it well is not. That gap between large and good is exactly what a diagnostic first session is for.

faqs.question: What does the free first lesson tell me about whether to spend anything at all?
faqs.answer: It produces a written diagnosis naming the strand, the specific error your child makes in it, and the cheapest tool that addresses it. For a substantial share of Dubai families that tool is daily practice or the school's intervention group, and the diagnosis is where the engagement ends. The lesson runs twenty-five minutes, which is the right length for a primary child, with no card details taken and nothing following automatically. You keep the document either way.

faqs.question: Should we wait until Year 7 before paying for any maths help?
faqs.answer: Waiting is right for a worry and wrong for a gap, and the difference is whether a teacher can name a strand and an error. A vague concern about a seven-year-old is usually a developmental range and paid help mostly buys the parent reassurance. A named fractions gap in Year 5 left until the second term of Year 7 resurfaces across four topics and costs three times as much to close. Year 6 is the best-timed primary purchase in Dubai; Year 1 is usually the worst.

faqs.question: Does the KHDA fee freeze change what we can afford for tutoring?
faqs.answer: For some families, materially. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there will be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for 2026-27, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. If your tutoring budget was going to be whatever the fee rise took, that money is now available. The useful response is to spend it deliberately on one named strand with an end point, rather than to convert it into a standing weekly slot nobody has diagnosed a need for.

faqs.question: What happens to the arrangement if we pause over the long Dubai summer?
faqs.answer: Nothing, because there is no term commitment to break. Blocks are bought as a number of sessions on a named strand, and a pause simply pauses them. For primary maths a summer gap costs more in fluency than in understanding, so the useful homework over a long break is ten minutes a day of practice rather than holiday sessions. Families who travel can keep sessions running on live video from any time zone if they would rather not break the rhythm.

faqs.question: Is a small group maths class cheaper per child, and does it work at primary age?
faqs.answer: Cheaper, yes, usually well below one-to-one rates. Effective, sometimes, but for a different problem. A group class delivers structure, routine and exposure, which is exactly right for a child whose issue is habit or attitude. It cannot address one child's specific misconception, because the teacher is managing five pupils at different points. The honest rule is that a group fixes behaviour around mathematics and one-to-one fixes mathematics, and buying the wrong one is a common and avoidable waste.

dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.closingHeading: Diagnose free, then buy one strand
dubai/ib-pyp-maths-tutor.closingBody: Before spending anything, ask your child's class teacher which of the five strands is weakest and what your child does when a question in it goes wrong. Then take the free 25-minute first lesson, which ends with a written diagnosis naming the strand, the error and the cheapest tool that would fix it. If that tool is ten minutes of daily practice rather than a paid block, we will tell you so and you will have lost nothing. Lessons run one-to-one on live video across the UAE, timed to Gulf Standard Time, in sessions short enough for a primary child to use.

intro.heading: What primary science support costs in Dubai, and what moves that number
paragraphs: Nobody in this market publishes a price for primary science. Three of the six pages that rank for Dubai tutoring queries quote no figure at all, and the two that do quote US dollars. So start with the hour. Across Dubai in late 2026, a university-student helper advertises from about AED 45 to AED 150, a qualified teacher working online sits between AED 150 and AED 300, a tutor who drives to your community charges AED 180 to AED 500 with the travel priced in, and a named or examiner-tier tutor can publish AED 650. Those are other providers' figures, dated and attributed in the table below. They are the market you are shopping in.

The second number is the one that decides whether the first one was worth paying. Primary science is not a syllabus with papers at the end of it. In the IB Primary Years Programme, science runs through the units of inquiry as conceptual content and as a set of skills: questioning, predicting, fair testing, recording, concluding. A Grade 3 child can score well on a worksheet about the water cycle and still believe that clouds are made of steam. A tutor who charges AED 220 an hour and leaves that belief intact has sold you nothing, however pleasant the hour was.

That is why a primary science hour is priced on a different thing from a Diploma hour. With a Diploma student you are buying content depth and examination technique against a published mark scheme. With a nine-year-old you are buying diagnosis. The teacher has to find the one sentence in your child's head that is wrong, build the correct chain of reasoning in the child's own words, and then get the child to write it down in a form a primary teacher would accept. A chemistry graduate who has never taught Year 4 can take an hour to discover that the problem is not science at all but the word 'because'.

Dubai adds three specific pressures to that. The emirate runs 227 private schools serving 387,441 students across seventeen curricula, and only about a fourteenth of that enrolment is on an International Baccalaureate programme, so an IB primary parent is a minority inside a majority-British and majority-Indian market. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees would not rise for 2026-27, which means household education budgets are, unusually, not being squeezed from that direction this year. And Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in every Dubai private school whatever its licensed curriculum, so a primary timetable is already fuller here than it would be in London or Mumbai.

What follows is the honest version. The AED bands with their sources. The four science strands and the misconception each one tends to leave behind. What really moves a quote up or down, with the question that tests each claim. Why your lesson runs on live video and what that saves you. And what the Year 6 step into MYP Sciences costs to close if you leave it until September.

dubai/ib-pyp-science-tutor.programmesIntro: An IB primary parent in Dubai is making decisions that reach past primary. These are the programmes a Dubai science learner moves through, and what each one changes about the kind of support worth buying.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Science is not timetabled as a separate subject in most PYP schools. It is carried inside six transdisciplinary themes, of which 'How the world works' is the science-heavy one, and it is assessed formatively through the work your child produces rather than by examination. Teachers report against learning outcomes and the approaches to learning, so a report can run to several pages without a single mark on it. Content is organised around key concepts such as form, function, causation and change.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the PYP sits inside a school that must also deliver Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and KHDA inspects the whole school annually on a six-band scale from Outstanding to Very Weak. Practically, that means your child's science week is shorter than the unit planner suggests, and an inspection report tells you about the school's teaching of science across a year group, not about your own child.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Sciences is marked against four criteria, each out of eight: knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The jump that catches Dubai families is not content but form. A child who has spent six years explaining ideas in conversation is suddenly marked on a written method, a table with units in the headers, a graph with a line of best fit and a paragraph that evaluates its own reliability.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run the full IB continuum, so a child can move from PYP to MYP without changing site. Others stop at Year 6, which means a transfer into a British Year 7 and a sudden split into Biology, Chemistry and Physics with separate teachers. The Dubai complication is timing: places in the continuum schools in Al Barsha and Mirdif move early, and the decision is usually made in the autumn of Year 5.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Diploma sciences each carry an internally assessed investigation worth a fifth of the final grade, plus written papers that reward precise command-term reading. Nothing about the Diploma needs to be bought at primary level. It matters here only because the skills that decide a Diploma science grade, mainly designing a fair test and writing an evaluation that names its own weaknesses, start forming in a PYP unit about melting ice.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, three of them International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places across the emirate. For a current PYP family that changes the odds on Diploma places in seven years' time, which is a reasonable thing to factor into a primary school decision and a poor reason to buy Diploma-level tutoring now.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: The alternative route out of primary in Dubai, taken by a large share of the emirate's enrolment. Science is sat either as three separate sciences, each with its own syllabus code, or as Coordinated or Combined Science. Papers are tiered: Core caps the grade, Extended opens the full range. It matters to a PYP parent because a move out of the IB continuum at Year 7 or Year 10 lands here.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools account for the largest share of Dubai private-school enrolment, so the IGCSE route is the one most of your child's neighbours are on. If you expect to transfer, the practical gap to close is written scientific method and the use of standard measurement, both of which a PYP child can practise years earlier at no extra cost.

dubai/ib-pyp-science-tutor.subjectsIntro: Primary science in the PYP is organised by strand and by skill rather than by subject. These are the pieces a tutor can actually work on with a Dubai primary learner, and what tends to be wrong inside each.

subjects.name: Living Things
subjects.description: Life cycles, habitats, classification, plant structure and, in the upper primary years, human body systems. The recurring problem is agency: children explain biology as though organisms choose. Seeds 'decide' to grow, plants 'eat' soil. A session replaces the story with a chain the child can say out loud, then checks it against a labelled diagram they draw themselves.

subjects.name: Materials and Matter
subjects.description: Properties of materials, solids, liquids and gases, mixing, dissolving, and reversible against irreversible change. Dissolving and melting collapse into one idea in most primary heads, and sugar stirred into water is widely believed to be gone. A kitchen scale and two weighings fix that in ten minutes, because the child sees conservation of mass rather than being told about it.

subjects.name: Forces and Energy
subjects.description: Push and pull, friction, magnetism, light, sound, simple circuits and energy transfer. Two beliefs survive almost every primary school: heavy things fall faster, and a battery holds electricity that is used up and disappears. Both are testable at home with objects a Dubai family already owns, which is why this strand works unusually well over video.

subjects.name: Earth and Space
subjects.description: Day and night, the seasons, the water cycle, rocks and soils, and weather. The seasons are the single most persistent error in primary science: children say summer is hotter because the Earth is closer to the sun, which in a Gulf climate is reinforced by lived experience. A lamp, a tilted globe and a screen share settles it.

subjects.name: Scientific Inquiry and Fair Testing
subjects.description: Asking a testable question, predicting with a reason, changing one variable, keeping the rest the same, and concluding from the measurement rather than from the expectation. This is the skill the MYP will mark and the PYP only reports on, so it is the highest-value thing a primary tutor can build. Most children can run a test and almost none can say what they held constant.

subjects.name: Measurement, Tables and Graphs
subjects.description: Reading a scale, choosing a sensible unit, repeating a reading, putting units in a table header rather than in every cell, and plotting with the independent variable on the horizontal axis. It looks like maths and is marked as science. A child who writes '14' with no unit loses the mark in the MYP and is simply corrected in the PYP, which is why it is never fixed.

subjects.name: Explanation Writing and Science Vocabulary
subjects.description: Turning a correct idea into a sentence a teacher can credit. The usual blocker is the connective: 'because', 'so that' and 'which means' are the difference between a description and an explanation. For English-as-an-additional-language learners, who are a large part of Dubai's primary intake, this is where the science mark is actually lost.

subjects.name: Design, Technology and Making
subjects.description: Building something to meet a stated need, testing it, then changing one feature and testing again. Dubai schools often run this inside 'How we organise ourselves' or a makerspace slot. The tutoring value is the iteration loop, because children build once, declare success and stop, which is exactly the habit the MYP design and evaluation criteria penalise.

subjects.name: Mathematics Inside Science
subjects.description: Averages from repeated readings, simple ratios, estimating before measuring, and reading between the marks on a scale. A surprising number of primary science errors are arithmetic errors wearing a lab coat. Diagnosing which of the two is failing takes one session and saves a term of the wrong support.

subjects.name: PYP Exhibition Research Skills
subjects.description: Choosing a line of inquiry narrow enough to answer, finding a source a ten-year-old can actually read, saying what the source is and who wrote it, and separating what was found from what was thought. A tutor may teach all of that. A tutor may not choose the question, write the text or make the slides, and this page says so for a reason.

dubai/ib-pyp-science-tutor.regionsTitle: Where Dubai PYP families book from, and what the school run does to a 4pm session
dubai/ib-pyp-science-tutor.regionsIntro: Session timing is the most practical thing an online tutor can get right, and it is set by where you live and which school your child attends. These are the communities most Dubai primary enquiries come from and what they mean for scheduling.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Al Barsha South
regions.note: The densest cluster of IB continuum schools in the emirate. Buses out of Al Barsha South can reach a Jumeirah villa well after 4pm in term time, so a Grade 2 child is frequently too tired for a 4pm slot; 5.15pm works far better and 6.30pm is too late.

regions.name: Emirates Hills, The Meadows and The Springs
regions.note: Long compound drives and a single gated entrance mean the gap between the bus arriving and a child sitting down is ten minutes, not two. Families here often prefer a 45-minute session at 5pm and a second shorter slot at the weekend rather than one long hour.

regions.name: Mirdif
regions.note: Short school runs and several IB continuum options nearby, so Mirdif families can genuinely start at 4pm. The constraint is the opposite one: siblings in different year groups and a single laptop, which is why back-to-back 45-minute slots are the common booking here.

regions.name: Al Jaddaf and Dubai Healthcare City
regions.note: Apartment living, so a quiet room for a science session has to be negotiated with the rest of the household. A headset and a cleared table matter more here than anywhere else in Dubai, and a 5.45pm slot after the younger sibling's bedtime routine tends to hold.

regions.name: The Sustainable City and Dubai Investments Park
regions.note: A long drive back from almost everywhere, which pushes sessions past 5.30pm during the week. These households are also the ones where an outdoor fair test is easiest to run, because the courtyards and the urban farm give a primary child something real to measure.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim, Al Safa and Jumeirah
regions.note: A mix of IB and British primary schools within a few minutes of each other, so cousins and neighbours are often on different curricula entirely. Parents here ask the most comparison questions, and the useful answer is usually about written method rather than content.

regions.name: Dubai Hills Estate and Nad Al Sheba
regions.note: Newer communities with newer schools and a lot of recent arrivals mid-year. A child who joined a PYP school in January from a different system is the typical enquiry, and the first session is usually diagnostic rather than taught.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: Close to several schools, so the commute is short and the 4pm slot is viable. Many families here are on a two-income schedule with no adult home before 7pm, which makes the weekend morning session the realistic one.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha, Al Barsha South and Emirates Hills
schoolClusters.note: The part of Dubai where an IB primary parent has the most choice and the most comparison to make. Several of these schools run the whole continuum from the early years to the Diploma, which changes the Year 6 conversation completely: the question becomes whether to stay rather than where to go.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Al Jaddaf and the southern communities
schoolClusters.note: A spread-out cluster where a PYP family's nearest school and their chosen school are often not the same place. Journeys are longer, sessions start later, and the enquiries skew towards upper primary and the Exhibition year rather than the early years.

dubai/ib-pyp-science-tutor.modesIntro: Primary science support comes in a small number of sensible shapes. Picking the wrong one is the commonest way a Dubai family spends money without changing anything.

modes.description: The default for a child between Year 1 and Year 5. Forty-five minutes is long enough to run a short fair test, talk through what happened and write two sentences about it, and short enough that a primary learner is still present at the end. The slot stays the same each week, in Gulf Standard Time, so it survives the school term rather than being renegotiated.

modes.description: Four to six sessions mapped onto one unit of inquiry, timed to finish a week before the summative assessment or the student-led conference. Useful when a report has flagged one area and the family does not want an open-ended commitment. The block starts with the school's central idea and lines of inquiry, and ends with the child explaining the unit back without notes.

The boundary is stated in advance and in writing, because the Exhibition is assessed as the child's own work and a tutor who crosses that line creates a problem for the school rather than solving one for you.

Two or three short sessions a week through July and August hold the ground rather than teaching new content, and they are the cheapest hours in the year to buy because nothing is urgent. Families moving schools in September use this slot to close a method gap before term starts.

sections.heading: What a Dubai parent is actually buying when they search for a PYP science tutor
paragraphs: An IB PYP science tutor in Dubai is a primary teacher who works inside your child's current unit of inquiry and is paid to find and fix a specific misunderstanding. Market rates for that, online and one-to-one, run roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour at the qualified-teacher tier as of October 2026. IB Gram delivers it as live video, one-to-one, in Gulf Standard Time. We do not offer home visits in the UAE; that is a service we run only in India, and this page is explicit about it rather than quiet.

The search phrase hides a decision most parents have not consciously made. There are three different purchases sitting behind it. The first is homework company: somebody to sit with a child while the unit sheet gets finished. The second is content catch-up: somebody to teach the science the child missed because they joined in January from another system. The third is skill building: somebody to make a nine-year-old competent at fair testing and written explanation so the MYP does not come as a shock. All three are legitimate. They cost different amounts, they take different numbers of weeks, and only one of them changes anything after the tutoring stops.

Dubai makes the first purchase unusually tempting, because the city is full of capable graduates willing to supervise homework for AED 60 an hour and the result looks like progress. Books get finished. Worksheets come back complete. Nothing in the child's reasoning has moved. The test for whether you bought the third thing instead is embarrassingly simple: ask your child to explain the last unit to you without the book, and listen for whether they use the word 'because' correctly.

The rest of this page is written to make that decision cheaply. The AED bands are published with their sources so you can compare any quote you receive. The strand table names the misconception each area of primary science tends to leave behind, so you can test a tutor's diagnosis in one question. And the section on the Year 6 step tells you what the gap costs to close if it is still open when MYP Sciences starts.

sections.heading: What primary science support costs in Dubai, band by band
paragraphs: Every figure in the table below was published by somebody else, and the right-hand column says who. None of them is an IB Gram price. We quote after a free trial lesson, because the honest answer depends on year group, how many weeks you want and whether the Exhibition is involved, and a fake single number would be less useful than the bands.

Read the bands as a function of two things: how much primary teaching experience you are buying, and whether anybody has to travel. The travel element is the largest single cause of price difference in this market. A tutor crossing Dubai at 4.30pm commits ninety minutes of their day to deliver sixty minutes of teaching, and that ratio is inside the AED 180 to AED 500 band whether or not it appears on the invoice. Online delivery removes it, which is why the qualified-teacher band online starts below where the in-home band starts.

The second pattern worth noticing is that the top of the market is a poor purchase at primary level. A tutor publishing AED 650 an hour is selling examination seniority. A seven-year-old who thinks dissolving and melting are the same thing does not need seniority; they need somebody who will put a kitchen scale on the table and weigh the glass twice. Spending at the top of the band in primary usually buys the wrong expertise at the right price.

A note on monthly packages, which is how a lot of Dubai providers prefer to sell. Advertised packages in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Divide before you compare: the second of those is a higher hourly rate than it looks, and two hours is far too long for a primary science session regardless of price.

sections.heading: Science in the PYP lives inside the units, not on the timetable
paragraphs: If you ask a Dubai PYP school when science happens, you may not get a time. In most PYP schools science is not a standalone lesson. It is conceptual content distributed through six transdisciplinary themes, and it surfaces most heavily in 'How the world works' and 'Sharing the planet'. A unit begins with a central idea, breaks into lines of inquiry, and finishes with a summative assessment that may be a presentation, a model or a piece of writing rather than a test. The science sits inside all of that, which is why a parent can read a whole report and not know whether their child understands evaporation.

This has a direct consequence for tutoring. A tutor who arrives with a generic primary science scheme is working against your school rather than with it. The useful first question from any provider is not 'what year group?' but 'what is the current central idea, and what are the lines of inquiry?'. Those two sentences are usually on the school's parent portal or in the termly unit letter. Hand them over before session one and the first hour is teaching rather than archaeology.

The second consequence concerns what gets assessed. Because the PYP reports against learning outcomes and the approaches to learning rather than marks, the thing your child is graded on in practice is the quality of their thinking made visible: the question they asked, the way they planned the test, the record they kept, the explanation they gave. A tutor can work on every one of those directly. Content gaps close quickly at primary level. Skill gaps do not, and they are the ones that follow a child into the MYP.

Worth knowing about Dubai specifically: because KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies in every private school whatever its licensed curriculum, the transdisciplinary week in a Dubai PYP classroom carries more fixed subject time than the IB framework alone implies. Teachers compress. Units that run six weeks elsewhere run five here. If your child is one of the slower processors in the room, that compression is frequently the real problem, and no amount of extra science content fixes it. Pace does.

sections.heading: The four science strands and the misconception each one leaves behind
paragraphs: Primary science misconceptions are unusually well documented and unusually consistent. The same wrong ideas appear in a Grade 4 classroom in Al Barsha and in a Year 4 classroom in Manchester, because they are sensible inferences from everyday experience rather than carelessness. That consistency is useful to a parent: it means you can test whether a tutor knows the territory by asking what they expect to find before they have met your child.

The table below sets out the four content strands as Dubai PYP schools generally cover them, the belief that tends to survive each one, and what a single session can do about it. The third column is the diagnostic one. A tutor who can name the misconception is a tutor who will look for it. A tutor who talks only about 'building confidence in science' will reteach the unit and leave the belief untouched.

The fifth row is the one that matters most over a child's school career. Scientific inquiry is a skill, not a topic, and in the PYP it is reported on rather than marked. It arrives in the MYP as two of the four assessment criteria, each worth eight marks, and by the Diploma it is a fifth of the grade. A child who learns at nine to change one variable and keep the rest the same is being given something that pays for a decade. That is the single best use of a primary science hour in this market, and almost nobody sells it, because it is harder to demonstrate to a parent than a finished worksheet.

One caution on how to use this table. Do not read it to your child as a list of things they have wrong. Primary misconceptions are dislodged by evidence the child collects, not by correction from an adult, and a nine-year-old told they are wrong about the seasons will simply learn to repeat the right words. The test of whether a misconception has actually gone is whether the child can predict correctly in a situation they have not seen before.

sections.heading: Doing real science over live video with what a Dubai kitchen already contains
paragraphs: The objection parents raise most often about online primary science is practical work, and it deserves a straight answer rather than reassurance. A video lesson is not a school laboratory and nobody should pretend otherwise. What it is, for primary science specifically, is better than most parents expect, because almost all PYP science practicals use household objects in the first place. Dubai apartments and villas contain everything the four strands need: a kitchen scale, measuring jugs, ice, salt, a torch, a few magnets, string, paper, a phone camera and a set of identical glasses.

The working method is simple and it changes who does the work. The tutor does not demonstrate while the child watches. The child sets the test up on their own table with the camera pointed at it, the tutor asks what is being changed and what is being kept the same, and the child takes the readings and says them out loud. This is the opposite of a classroom practical, where one confident child usually handles the apparatus and the rest observe. A one-to-one video session makes passivity impossible, which is the real argument for it at primary level.

There are genuine limits and it is better to name them. Anything requiring a flame, a chemical beyond kitchen vinegar and bicarbonate, a microscope or a sealed electrical supply is out. Dissection is out. Precision measurement below a gram or a millimetre is out. For a PYP child none of those exclusions bites, because the strands do not require them. By MYP Sciences they begin to, and that is one of the honest reasons a secondary science student needs their school laboratory and not only a tutor.

A short safety note that matters in a Dubai household. Sessions never involve the child using the hob, hot water above hand temperature, sharp blades or anything from a cleaning cupboard. Where a step needs an adult, the session plan says so in advance so a parent or a household helper can be nearby for two minutes rather than for the whole lesson. Apparatus lists go out the day before, so nothing is hunted for during paid time.

sections.heading: Seven things that move a Dubai primary science quote, and the question that tests each
paragraphs: Quotes for primary tutoring in Dubai vary by a factor of ten for work that looks identical in an advert. Most of that spread is explicable, and every item in the table below is something you can ask about on a phone call before any money moves. The fourth column is the point: each question has an answer that either lands immediately or does not, and a provider who cannot answer in a sentence is usually not pricing what they think they are pricing.

The item parents underestimate is planning time. A tutor who reads your school's unit planner, central idea and lines of inquiry before the first session is spending unpaid time to make the paid time work. Some providers bill that visibly, some absorb it into the hourly rate, and some simply do not do it. All three are defensible positions. What is not defensible is a provider who claims to plan from the school's unit and then opens a generic workbook in session one, which you will know about within ten minutes.

The item parents overestimate is the sibling discount. Two children in the same household share the administration of a booking and almost none of the teaching, so an honest household rate is modest. A provider offering half price for a second child is either padding the first price or planning to teach two different year groups in one session, which at primary level produces two half-taught children rather than one well-taught one.

Finally, the Exhibition premium is real and it is not about difficulty. The final primary year carries an assessed piece of work that must be the student's own, and supervising that properly means knowing exactly where teaching stops. A tutor who charges more for Exhibition-year support and can tell you in advance what they will refuse to do is pricing judgement. A tutor who charges the same and offers to 'help put the presentation together' is cheaper for a reason you do not want.

sections.heading: A tutor driving across Dubai against 45 minutes on live video
paragraphs: This page targets a search a lot of Dubai parents type, and some of them mean a person in the room. The honest position is worth stating in full. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service we run only in India, and nothing on this page should be read as an offer of one. What we run for Dubai families is one-to-one live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, with the same tutor each week. The comparison below is not a sales argument dressed as a table; the in-home option wins two of the five rows.

Where a visiting tutor genuinely wins is physical presence with a very young or very distractible child, and the ability to look at a messy exercise book without anybody photographing it. For a child in FS2 or Year 1 who cannot yet read independently, an adult in the room is a real advantage and we would rather say so than pretend otherwise. By Year 3 the advantage has usually inverted, because what the child needs is the right teacher rather than the nearest one.

Where online wins is tutor matching and schedule survival. The pool of people who can teach PYP science well and will drive to Dubai Investments Park for a 4.30pm slot is small. The pool who can teach it well on video is not. Over a term, the second difference compounds: a session that needs no travel gets rescheduled inside the same week when a swimming gala appears, and a session that needs a car across Al Khail Road at 4pm is usually lost.

On cost, the arithmetic is not subtle. The Dubai in-home band published by other providers runs AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel inside it. The online qualified-teacher band runs AED 150 to AED 300. For a family budgeting a fixed monthly figure, that difference is typically two or three extra sessions a term, or the same number of sessions with a better-matched teacher. Both are better outcomes than a shorter commute for an adult who is not your child.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies around a primary science week
paragraphs: Dubai parents often discover the mandatory subjects only when a report arrives with an Arabic grade on it. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must follow the Ministry's general regulations. KHDA's own mandatory-subject guidance requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with those requirements implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year.

Two details in that guidance change how a primary week actually feels. First, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for the two groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Second, the required instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and the guidance advises that any mandatory subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes. That is a real block of fixed time inside a transdisciplinary timetable.

KHDA also requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education and for Arabic as a first language, and Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, with the school's licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies. And teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic are required to hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. For the mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, which is why a tutor should work from the school's own material in these subjects rather than importing a scheme.

What this means for a science-focused tutoring plan is mostly about sequencing. If a child is struggling in Arabic as an additional language and in written science explanation at the same time, the language work usually comes first, because the science mark in a Dubai primary classroom is frequently lost in the sentence rather than in the idea. Where a family wants both, it is better bought as two specialists in two slots than as one hour that claims to cover both.

sections.heading: From PYP science into MYP Sciences: the Year 6 step and what it costs to close late
paragraphs: The handover out of primary is where most of the money in this market is eventually spent, and almost all of it is spent later than it needed to be. A PYP child arrives in MYP Sciences having spent years explaining ideas out loud and being reported on narratively. They are then marked against four criteria out of eight each, two of which are about designing an investigation and processing its results. The content is not the problem. The form is.

Concretely, here is what changes in the first term of Year 7 for a child who has come through the PYP. Method has to be written before the practical rather than described after it. Tables need units in the headings. Graphs need axes chosen by the student, with the independent variable on the horizontal axis and a line of best fit rather than dot-to-dot. Conclusions have to refer to the data and then say what was unreliable about it. Each of those is a small, teachable, mechanical skill. Together they are the difference between a 4 and a 6 in the first reporting cycle, and they have nothing to do with how well the child understands science.

The cost asymmetry is the argument for doing it early. In the final primary year, this is one strand of an ordinary weekly session at the primary rate, folded into work the child is already doing. In the first term of MYP, it becomes remedial work at the secondary rate, competing with new content, while the child is also adjusting to separate teachers and a timetable. Families who close the method gap in Year 6 generally stop tutoring in Year 7. Families who wait usually do not.

For Dubai families there is a second version of this step: leaving the IB continuum at Year 7 for a British-curriculum school, which is a common move here given how much of the emirate's enrolment is British-curriculum. That transition needs the same written method work plus a vocabulary shift, because the receiving school will split science into Biology, Chemistry and Physics with three teachers and an expectation of subject-specific terminology from the first week. The preparation is identical. Only the destination changes.
